text: Build a Trie class. Insert adds a word. Search returns true if that exact word was inserted. Starts with returns true if any inserted word starts with the given prefix.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — search and starts with do the same walk down the tree. The only difference is the last check. Search needs the walk to end on a real word. Starts with only needs the walk to not fall off. Is that right?
Are there any constraints on the input size? And is it only lowercase letters?
Words and prefixes are one to two thousand characters long. Lowercase English letters only. At most three times ten to the fourth calls in total.

Okay. Lowercase only means each node can hold a fixed array of twenty-six child pointers — no hash map needed. Let me run through the example. Insert apple, and search apple is true. Search app is false, because app was never inserted as a word, but starts with app is true. Then insert app, and now search app is true. So the output is null, null, true, false, true, null, true. That matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to keep every word in a list. Then starts with has to check every stored word, so the cost grows with the number of words, not with the length of the prefix. A hash set makes search fast, but it can't answer prefix questions at all. This problem reminds me of the prefix tree behind autocomplete. Words that share a start should share the same path. Each edge is one letter, and each node is one prefix, so every call costs only the length of its string.

Here's the plan. One: each node has twenty-six child slots, all null, plus an is-word flag. Two: insert walks the word, creates a child only when the slot is empty, then marks the last node. Three: search does the same walk and fails if it falls off; at the end, prefix mode returns true and word mode returns is-word. Starts with just calls search with prefix set to true. The flag matters because a node existing only means some word passes through it. One thing worth flagging — the null check in insert is a correctness rule, not a speed trick. If I always created a new node, inserting app after apple would replace the old path and cut off the l and e nodes, so search apple would return false. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. A trie node holds twenty-six child pointers, all starting as null, and an is-word flag. Insert creates a child only when its slot is null, steps down, and marks the last node. Search returns false the moment a child is missing; after the loop it returns true in prefix mode, otherwise is-word. One thing worth flagging — starts with reuses search through a default argument, bool prefix equals false. LeetCode only calls search with one argument, so the public behavior stays the same. The only difference is the last line: in prefix mode I return true before I look at is-word.

Let's dry-run the code with the official example. Expected: null, null, true, false, true, null, true. The two rows that matter are search app and starts with app. They do the same walk and end on the same node. Search says false because no word ends there yet; starts with says true because the path exists. Then insert app creates zero new nodes — we stay at six — and only flips the flag. That's the null check keeping the apple nodes attached. That matches. Corner cases: search apx walks to a, p, finds no x child, and returns false. Starts with apple is true, because a word counts as a prefix of itself.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear in L per call, for insert, search and starts with, where L is the string length. It doesn't depend on how many words are stored. Space is total inserted characters times twenty-six pointers. In the worst case no words share a prefix, so every character makes a new node, and each node carries twenty-six slots. Oh, one more thing — there's no destructor, so the nodes are never freed. That's fine on LeetCode. In real code I'd add a destructor that deletes children recursively, or keep the nodes in unique pointers or a pool.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You saw early that search and starts with are the same walk with a different last check, and you shared one loop for both. You explained that the null check in insert is about correctness, because overwriting a child would cut off existing words. And your dry-run showed insert app making zero new nodes, which proves the old subtree stays safe. Good work.
